opts: .NET is a framework for writing C#
C# is a language that targets the .NET platform
.NET and C# are two names for the same thing
C# compiles directly to machine code
0.expl: .NET is the platform — runtime, libraries, tooling. C# is one language that targets it, alongside F# and VB.NET. C# compiles to IL, not machine code.

0.q: What does the C# compiler produce?
opts: Machine code for the current CPU
0.expl: Roslyn produces IL, a portable instruction set. The CLR then JIT-compiles IL to native code at runtime, which is what makes the same binary portable across operating systems.

0.q: Which of these is the legacy, Windows-only line?
0.expl: .NET Framework (up to 4.8) is Windows-only and receives no new feature versions. .NET Core and the unified .NET 5+ are cross-platform.

0.q: Why did Microsoft skip .NET 4 when renaming?
opts: It was released only in Asia
0.expl: .NET Framework already had 4.x versions. Releasing a unified '.NET 4' would have been ambiguous, so they went straight to .NET 5.

0.q: Which is the ASP.NET Core equivalent in the Java world?
0.expl: ASP.NET Core is the web framework ↔ Spring Boot. Entity Framework Core ↔ Hibernate/JPA. NuGet ↔ Maven Central. CLR ↔ JVM.

1.q: You can run a .NET app but dotnet build says no SDK was found. What happened?
opts: You installed the runtime, not the SDK
The target framework is too new
1.expl: The runtime only executes apps. The SDK contains the compiler and build tooling. For development you want the SDK — it includes a runtime too.

1.q: Why does a .csproj not list the source files?
opts: It does, in a hidden section
The SDK includes every .cs file in the folder tree by default
Files must be registered with dotnet add file
1.expl: Modern SDK-style projects glob all .cs files beneath the project folder. This is why .csproj files are short compared with old .NET Framework ones, which listed every file explicitly.

opts: Publishes a release build and runs it
1.expl: All three steps. Convenient, but it means a failure could be a restore, compile or runtime problem — read which stage the error came from.

1.q: A project has two files with top-level statements. Result?
opts: A warning; the first is used
1.expl: The compiler needs exactly one entry point. Two compilation units with top-level statements is an error, not a warning.

1.q: Which command would you use to measure performance meaningfully?
1.expl: Debug is the default and disables optimisations while adding instrumentation. Timing a Debug build produces numbers that do not reflect production.

2.q: Which type should hold an account balance?
2.expl: decimal is base-10 and represents decimal fractions exactly. double is base-2 and introduces rounding error that compounds across many operations.
var is compile-time type inference, not dynamic typing. x is int permanently. (The dynamic keyword exists and does defer to runtime, but that is not var.)

2.q: What does maybe!.Length do when maybe is null?
2.expl: The ! operator only silences the compiler warning. It performs no check, so dereferencing null still throws at runtime. It converts a compile-time warning into a runtime crash.
const requires a compile-time constant. DateTime.UtcNow is evaluated at runtime, so it needs static readonly instead.

3.q: Why does if (count) fail to compile when count is an int?
opts: C# requires the condition to be bool
Only bools can be local variables
3.expl: C# has no truthiness. A condition must be of type bool, which removes the family of bugs that comes from implicit numeric-to-boolean conversion.
Modifying a collection during enumeration invalidates the enumerator and throws InvalidOperationException. Iterate a copy, or use list.RemoveAll(x => x < 0).
3.code:
foreach (var x in list)
    if (x < 0) list.Remove(x);

3.q: Which is true of C#'s switch statement but not C's or Java's?
opts: Implicit fall-through is a compile error
3.expl: Every non-empty case must end in break, return or throw. Stacking empty case labels is still allowed, but silently falling from one body into the next is not.

3.q: What is the main advantage of a switch expression over a switch statement?
opts: It produces a value and the compiler checks exhaustiveness
It can match on types only
3.expl: Being an expression means it must yield a value on every path, so the compiler warns about unhandled cases. Adding a new enum member then surfaces every place you need to update.

opts: Any object with those property names
An object whose Source.Currency equals NGN and whose Amount exceeds 1000
3.expl: A property pattern tests the values of properties, including nested ones via dotted paths. All listed conditions must hold for the arm to match.

4.q: What is value inside a property setter?
opts: A contextual keyword holding the incoming assignment
4.expl: value is supplied by the compiler and represents whatever is being assigned. You never declare it, and it only exists inside a setter (or an init accessor).

4.q: Which allows a property to be set during construction but never afterwards?
4.expl: init permits assignment in a constructor or object initialiser and forbids it afterwards. { get; } alone cannot be set by an object initialiser at all; private set allows changes from inside the class at any time.

opts: Makes the compiler reject construction that omits the property
4.expl: It is a compile-time guarantee: object creation that does not set the property is a compile error. No runtime check and no constructor needed.

4.q: Two Account objects have identical property values. What does a == b return by default?
4.expl: Classes use reference equality by default — equal only if they are the same object. To compare by value you override Equals and GetHashCode, or use a record.

4.q: Why is a static int _counter risky in a web API?
opts: It is shared across all concurrent requests and can race
It cannot be read from instance methods
4.expl: There is one copy per process, shared by every request thread. Unsynchronised increments can interleave and produce duplicate or skipped values under load.

5.q: A base class has public decimal Fee() (not virtual). A derived class declares public decimal Fee(). What happens?
opts: It hides the base method; calls via a base reference run the base version
5.expl: Without virtual/override you get method hiding, not overriding. A base-typed reference calls the base implementation. The compiler warns and suggests the new keyword if hiding was intended.

5.q: Which is true of interfaces in C#?
opts: A class can implement many of them
5.expl: Single class inheritance, multiple interface implementation. Interfaces have no instance fields and no constructors — they describe a capability, not storage.

5.q: What does a == b return for two records with identical values?
5.expl: Records have generated value equality based on their components. This is the main behavioural difference from a class, which uses reference equality by default.

5.q: What does var c = a with { Amount = 250m }; do?
opts: Creates a copy of a with Amount changed, leaving a untouched
5.expl: The with expression performs non-destructive mutation: a new instance copying all members except those listed. The original is immutable and unchanged.

5.q: Which best fits an API request payload?
5.expl: A request payload is data with no identity or lifecycle. A record gives value equality, immutability, a generated ToString and concise syntax — exactly what a DTO wants.

6.expl: Where is deferred. The query runs when Count() enumerates it, by which time the list holds 1,2,3,4 — so three items are greater than 1. Calling ToList() before the Add would have given 2.

6.q: map["missing"] on a Dictionary where the key is absent:
6.expl: The indexer throws on a missing key when reading. TryGetValue returns false and supplies default(V) via out. (Assigning through the indexer does add the key.)

6.q: A loop calls list.Contains(x) on each of n items. Complexity?
6.expl: List.Contains is O(n), inside an O(n) loop, so O(n²). Changing the collection to a HashSet makes Contains O(1) and the whole thing O(n) — usually a one-line fix.

6.q: Which does NOT force immediate execution?
6.expl: Select is deferred — it describes a transformation. ToList, Count and Any all enumerate the sequence at once.

6.q: You look up a user by primary key and expect exactly one. Which is most appropriate?
6.expl: Single states the assumption that exactly one row matches and throws if there are more — surfacing a data-integrity problem instead of silently taking the first. Use SingleOrDefault if zero matches is also legitimate.

7.q: What is wrong with catch (Exception ex) { throw ex; }?
opts: It resets the stack trace to the catch block
7.expl: throw ex restarts the exception from this line, discarding the frames that show where the problem actually occurred. Bare throw; rethrows with the original trace intact.

7.q: A caller passes a negative amount to Deposit. Which exception fits best?
7.expl: The argument itself is invalid and out of its permitted range. InvalidOperationException would be for a valid argument that is wrong for the object's current state.

opts: It runs only if no exception occurred
It runs only if an exception occurred
It runs on success, on exception, and on early return
7.expl: finally always runs on the way out of the block, which is why it is the right place to release resources. using is syntactic sugar over exactly this pattern.

7.q: Why prefer when (ex.StatusCode == ...) over an if inside the catch?
opts: If the filter is false the exception is never caught, leaving the stack intact for an outer handler
if is not allowed in a catch
7.expl: A failed filter means the catch does not run at all, so the exception continues to propagate with its original stack and the debugger still breaks at the throw site. An if inside the catch has already unwound the stack.

7.q: Insufficient funds on a withdrawal is best modelled as:
opts: An exception, since it is a failure
A normal return value or result type, since it is an expected outcome
7.expl: It is a predictable business outcome, not an exceptional condition. Using exceptions for expected results is expensive and obscures the normal path. (A domain exception is still reasonable at a lower layer if callers must react differently — the judgement is whether it is expected.)

8.q: What is the main benefit of async/await in a web API?
opts: Threads are freed while waiting on I/O, raising concurrent throughput
It removes the need for locks
8.expl: An individual request is not faster — often marginally slower. The gain is that a thread is not held while waiting on I/O, so a fixed thread pool can serve many more simultaneous requests.

8.q: Why should you never write async void?
opts: Exceptions cannot be caught by the caller and crash the process
8.expl: An async void method cannot be awaited, so the caller has no handle to observe completion or failure. Exceptions escape to the runtime and bring down the process. Event handlers are the one forced exception.

8.q: How long does this take, given each call is 200ms?
8.expl: The calls start when invoked, not when awaited, so all three are in flight before WhenAll. Total time is roughly the slowest one. Awaiting each in turn instead would give 600ms.

8.q: Which is the correct way to call an async method from a synchronous one?
opts: Make the calling method async and await
8.expl: All three blocking forms risk deadlock and waste a thread. The answer is async all the way up — change the caller's signature. If a framework boundary forbids it, that boundary is the problem to solve.

8.q: You wrap an HTTP call in Task.Run. What happens?
opts: A pool thread is occupied doing nothing but waiting
8.expl: Task.Run schedules work on a pool thread. For I/O there is no CPU work to schedule, so you have taken a thread out of the pool purely to wait — exactly what async avoids. Task.Run is for CPU-bound work.

9.q: In Func<string, int, bool>, what does the method return?
9.expl: In Func the last type parameter is always the return type; the ones before it are parameters. So this takes a string and an int and returns a bool. Action has no return type parameter at all.
All three lambdas captured the same variable i, not its value at the time. The loop finished with i equal to 3, so each prints 3. Copying into a per-iteration variable fixes it.

9.q: Which delegate type takes one argument and returns nothing?
9.expl: Action<T> takes a T and returns void. Func<T> takes nothing and returns a T. Predicate<T> takes a T and returns bool.

9.q: Why use ?.Invoke() when raising an event?
opts: An event with no subscribers is null
9.expl: With no subscribers the backing delegate field is null, so a direct call throws NullReferenceException. The null-conditional invoke handles that case.

9.q: Injecting Func<DateTime> instead of calling DateTime.UtcNow directly mainly buys you:
opts: Testability — a test can control the time
9.expl: Code calling DateTime.UtcNow directly cannot be tested deterministically for anything time-dependent. Injecting the clock as a delegate lets a test supply a fixed value.

11.q: You inject a Scoped DbContext into a Singleton service. What happens?
opts: The DbContext is shared across all requests for the app's lifetime
A new DbContext is created per request anyway
11.expl: A captive dependency. The singleton captures the first scoped instance and keeps it forever, so a request-scoped object outlives its request — causing disposed-object errors and data leaking between users.

11.q: Which lifetime should a repository normally use?
11.expl: Scoped — one instance per HTTP request. That matches the DbContext lifetime it usually depends on and keeps per-request state isolated. Scoped is the sensible default for application services.

11.q: What does middleware do if it never calls next?
opts: Short-circuits the pipeline and returns the response immediately
11.expl: Not calling next ends the pipeline there and the response travels back out. This is deliberate and is how rate limiting, caching and short-circuit auth failures are implemented.

opts: Authorisation runs before the user is identified, so authenticated endpoints reject valid requests
11.expl: The pipeline runs in registration order. Authorisation needs an identity to evaluate; if authentication has not run yet there is none, so everything looks unauthenticated.

11.q: Where should a database password live?
opts: User secrets in development, environment variables or a secret store in production
11.expl: appsettings.json is committed to source control. dotnet user-secrets keeps development values off disk in the repo, and production should read from the environment or a managed secret store.

12.q: A request arrives authenticated but the user lacks permission. Correct status?
12.expl: 403 Forbidden — identity is known, permission is denied, and retrying with the same credentials will not help. 401 means not authenticated at all.

12.q: Why not bind a POST body directly to an EF entity?
opts: A client can set any property, including ones it should not
12.expl: Over-posting. The model binder sets whatever properties appear in the JSON, so a client could include Balance or IsAdmin. DTOs define exactly what may be supplied.

12.q: With [ApiController], what happens when a model fails data-annotation validation?
opts: Your action runs with invalid data
A 400 with ValidationProblemDetails is returned before your action runs
12.expl: [ApiController] adds automatic model-state validation. The 400 response with a per-field problem document is produced before your method is entered.

12.q: A POST successfully creates a resource. Best response?
opts: 201 with a Location header pointing at the new resource
12.expl: 201 Created with a Location header is the REST convention. CreatedAtAction generates the header from a named action. (202 is correct when creation is genuinely asynchronous and not yet complete.)

12.q: Why handle exceptions in middleware rather than per controller?
opts: It is the only way that works
Consistent error shape, one place to change, and internal messages cannot leak
12.expl: Centralising translation gives every endpoint the same error contract, keeps HTTP concerns out of business logic, and means you decide once what detail is safe to expose.

13.q: Which of these loads the entire table into memory?
13.expl: In b, ToListAsync executes first, so every row crosses the network and the filter runs in your process. Everything before ToListAsync is translated to SQL; everything after is LINQ-to-objects.
13.code:
var a = await _db.Accounts.Where(x => x.Balance > 1000).ToListAsync();
var b = (await _db.Accounts.ToListAsync()).Where(x => x.Balance > 1000);

13.q: Why must DbContext be Scoped rather than Singleton?
opts: It is slower as a Singleton
It is not thread-safe and accumulates tracked entities
EF forbids it at compile time
13.expl: A DbContext represents one unit of work. It is not thread-safe, so concurrent requests corrupt it, and it tracks every entity it loads, so a long-lived one grows unboundedly and serves stale data.

13.q: 1,000 accounts, and the loop reads a.Transactions.Count on each. How many queries?
13.expl: The N+1 problem: one query for the accounts plus one per account for its transactions. Include() makes it a single joined query, or project the count so the database computes it.

13.q: What does SaveChangesAsync guarantee about multiple changes?
opts: They are applied in one transaction — all or none
13.expl: SaveChanges wraps all pending changes in a single transaction. This is why a transfer touching two accounts plus a transaction record is atomic without you managing it.

opts: When you will modify the entities
13.expl: Change tracking costs memory and time setting up snapshots. For a read-only query — a report, a list view — AsNoTracking skips it. Do not use it when you intend to modify and save the entities, because changes will not be detected.

14.q: Is the payload of a JWT encrypted?
opts: No — it is base64-encoded and readable by anyone holding the token
14.expl: A JWT is signed, not encrypted. The signature proves integrity, not confidentiality. Anyone with the token can decode and read every claim, so nothing sensitive belongs in one.

14.q: Why can't you revoke a JWT?
opts: It is validated by signature alone, with no server lookup
Only the client can revoke it
14.expl: Stateless validation is the whole point — any server with the key can verify a token without consulting a store. The cost is that nothing can mark it invalid, so you use short lifetimes plus a revocable refresh token.

14.q: A user is authenticated but lacks the required claim. Which status?
14.expl: 403 Forbidden — identity established, permission denied. 401 is for a missing or invalid token, where authenticating again could help.

14.q: Which is an acceptable password hash?
14.expl: bcrypt is deliberately slow with a tunable work factor and a per-user salt. SHA-256 and MD5 are fast by design, which suits checksums and ruins password storage. Encryption is wrong in principle: anything reversible means a key compromise exposes every password.

opts: Nothing, it just speeds things up
Tokens with any signature are accepted, so anyone can forge one
14.expl: Without verifying the signature against your key, a token's claims can be anything an attacker writes — including an admin role. This flag exists to be left alone.

15.q: Which log call supports querying by amount later?
15.expl: B keeps the message template constant and attaches Amount as a structured field, so an aggregator can group identical events and filter on the value. A produces a unique string each time and nothing queryable.
15.code:
A: _logger.LogInformation($"Transfer of {amount} done");
B: _logger.LogInformation("Transfer of {Amount} done", amount);

15.q: Log placeholders are matched to arguments by:
15.expl: Positionally. The names are for the output and for querying, not for binding — so swapping two arguments silently mislabels both values.

15.q: Which is correct for logging an exception?
15.expl: The exception is the first argument with no matching placeholder, which preserves the full stack trace. ex.Message alone discards the stack and is often unhelpful or empty.

15.q: Why should liveness not check the database?
opts: A database blip would make the orchestrator kill healthy instances
15.expl: Liveness answers 'is this process working'. If it fails on a dependency outage, every instance is restarted during exactly the incident when you need them — converting a degradation into an outage. Dependency checks belong in readiness.

opts: Serialising the object writes every field, including sensitive ones
15.expl: The whole object is serialised, so any PII, card number or token it holds lands in the log file. Log the specific named fields you actually need instead.

16.q: You need the same test to run against five different input values. Use:
16.expl: A Theory with InlineData reports each case as its own test, so you see exactly which input failed. A loop inside one Fact stops at the first failure and tells you less.

16.q: Why is mocking DbContext directly a bad idea?
opts: Tests end up asserting your assumptions about EF rather than real behaviour
16.expl: You do not own EF's semantics — tracking, deferred execution, SQL translation. A mock encodes what you think it does. Wrap it behind your own interface, or use an integration test against a real provider.

16.q: xUnit creates a new instance of the test class:
16.expl: Per test. That is why the constructor works as setup and why no state leaks between tests. Shared expensive setup is opted into explicitly with IClassFixture.

16.q: Which is the most valuable test for a payment service?
opts: A property setter stores the value
A timed-out core banking call does not debit twice
16.expl: The failure paths are both the hardest to produce by hand and where the costly bugs live. The happy path is usually exercised constantly by ordinary use; the timeout-retry-double-debit case is not.

16.q: A test breaks when you rename a private method, with behaviour unchanged. That means:
opts: The test is coupled to implementation rather than behaviour
16.expl: Tests should assert what the code does, not how. One that breaks on an internal rename makes refactoring expensive, which is the opposite of what a test suite is for.
